The empirical record across independent disciplines supplies convergent support for the prediction across multiple temporal scales. Comparative cognition documents the depth threshold the parent section identified. Animal tool-use is widespread — sea otters cracking shellfish on stone anvils carried between feedings, chimpanzees stripping twigs to fish termites, New Caledonian crows manufacturing hooked tools and remembering which tools worked on which kinds of larvae, octopuses carrying coconut shells across the seafloor to assemble shelter (Goodall 1968; Hunt 1996; Finn, Tregenza, and Norman 2009; Rutz et al. 2010). What none of these cases demonstrates is *cumulative* culture in the strong sense — the modification of inherited tools across generations such that later cohorts build on improvements they did not invent. Chimpanzee termite-fishing has remained essentially the same across the decades it has been observed; corvid tool techniques do not accumulate refinement across cohorts. Cumulative culture — a practice that *gets better* across generations because each cohort inherits not raw technique but a tradition already under modification — is rare-to-absent below the recursive depth that lets a subject model not only the tool but the practice of tool-modification, the reasoning that produced the modification, and the transmission that carries it forward (Tomasello 1999; Boyd, Richerson, and Henrich 2011; Henrich 2015; Laland 2017). The threshold the parent section names is the threshold below which redirection of the medium does not compound, and above which it does. Below it, redirection occurs at a single level; above it, redirection itself becomes subject to redirection, and the recursion's reach into structure begins to compound.

The archaeological record shows the threshold being crossed. Tool use in the hominin lineage predates anatomically modern humans by over two million years — Plummer et al. (2023, *Science*) secure Oldowan tools (the earliest stone-tool tradition) at 2.9 million years from Nyayanga, Kenya; the earlier Lomekwi 3.3-million-year claim (Harmand et al. 2015) has been contested on dating and assemblage grounds (Domínguez-Rodrigo and Alcalá 2016), but Plummer et al. (2023) secure the broader claim independent of that dispute. The threshold for some redirection is well below *sapiens*. Fire control appears by at least 400,000 years ago. Agriculture emerges independently across at least seven distinct regions between roughly 10,000 and 5,000 BCE (Diamond 1997) — precisely what the necessary-emergence principle predicts: not a single invention diffusing outward but the same threshold reached independently wherever the structural conditions were met. Writing emerges independently in Mesopotamia, China, and Mesoamerica. Each emergence is the same recursion crossing the same threshold under independent conditions, because the threshold is a feature of what self-modeling-deep-enough-to-redirect *is*, not of any particular cultural lineage. The pattern supports recurrence under similar pressures rather than strict necessity: which subjects cross the threshold first, in what form, and at what timing remain shaped by historical contingencies — geography, available materials, climate, demographic scale, neighboring traditions, sequencing of prior crossings. The structural prediction is that the threshold gets crossed wherever the conditions hold long enough; the contingencies determine the path each crossing takes.

The acceleration of technological elaboration over the past three centuries is consistent with the recurrence the account predicts once people model their conditions explicitly and acquire the material and social capacity to act on those models at scale. The Industrial Revolution developed through increasingly precise control of energy gradients; the digital revolution through the representation and manipulation of information in new substrates; artificial intelligence through attempts to model and reproduce increasingly complex forms of inference and self-modeling. These histories do not show that any particular revolution, timing, or technical form was necessary. They support the narrower claim that technological reach compounds when inherited representations, instruments, and institutions allow later work to operate on the products of earlier work. Historical contingencies determine which developments occur, where they occur, and who controls them.

*Device-form and focal practice.* The same acceleration distinguishes two forms technology takes under conditions of rapid externalization. The device paradigm (Borgmann 1984) names the characteristic modern form: technology that delivers a commodity — warmth, entertainment, food, information, computation — while concealing the machinery and disburdening the user of engagement with what produces it. The hearth becomes the furnace, the meal becomes the microwave, the concert becomes the playlist. What changes is not the output but the focal practice: the skilled, attentive engagement with the thing itself that the earlier form required, and that structured communal life around it. The structural account locates the device-form as what the recursion produces when externalization scales faster than depth deepens — a predictable attractor rather than a pathology. The focal-practice form remains available where counter-practices are cultivated at sufficient depth; the two forms coexist wherever the conditions for both are present.
